result.markdown: --- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.constraint()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Edgecase description: Calculate Burt's constraint for each node. twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.constraint()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Edgecase description: Calculate Burt's constraint for each node. title: >- [Graph.constraint()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: Calculate Burt's constraint for each node. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Calculate Burt's constraint for each node. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L44712-L44885){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.constraint( weights=None, attr_name=None, return_dict=False, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Burt's constraint](/assets/graphs/constraint.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="The shared seven-node strip of triangles with a tail, shaded by Burt's constraint. The pendant G, with a single contact, is fully constrained at 1.00, and A, whose two contacts know each other, follows at 0.84. The bridge E, linking the triangles to the tail, spans a structural hole and has the lowest constraint, 0.48." width="100%"} Burt's constraint measures the extent to which ego's contacts are redundant, that is, connected to each other. Higher constraint indicates fewer structural holes and less brokerage opportunity. Lower constraint indicates a network position with more non-redundant contacts, offering greater access to diverse information and control benefits. The constraint of node i's ego network is: `C_i = Σ_j (p_ij + Σ_q p_iq × p_qj)²` where `p_ij` are proportional tie strengths: `p_ij = (a_ij + a_ji) / Σ_k (a_ik + a_ki)` and `a_ij` are elements of the adjacency matrix (edge weights). The sums run over the node's contacts, its neighbors in either direction; on a directed graph that includes in-neighbors, so a node with only incoming edges still gets a value (NetworkX returns `nan` for it). Results otherwise match `networkx.constraint()`. Time complexity: `O(V × D²)` where `D` is average degree Space complexity: `O(V)` ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [weights]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of the edge attribute to use as tie strength. If `None` (default) or `"weight"`, the edge's weight field is used. Edges without a (numeric) value count as `1.0`, so on an unweighted graph all ties are equal. Parallel edges add up their weights; on a directed graph `a_ij` and `a_ji` are the arcs in each direction. [attr_name]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of the node attribute to store constraint values. If `None`, uses `constraint` as the attribute name. [return_dict]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, returns a dictionary mapping node IDs to constraint values. If `False`, stores values as node attributes and returns the Graph for chaining. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict[int, float | None] or Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `return_dict=` is `True`, a dictionary mapping node IDs to constraint values is returned. Returns `None` for isolated nodes, including nodes whose only edge is a self-loop (undefined constraint, `nan` in NetworkX). If `return_dict=` is `False`, returns self for method chaining. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} A constraint value close to $1$ says ego's contacts are tightly interlinked, so any one tie is largely redundant with the others: high closure, little room for brokerage. Values approaching $0$ mark the opposite regime: ego's contacts sit in structural holes, disconnected from one another, and information or influence flowing between them must pass through ego. Burt (1992) formalizes this as $c_i = \sum_j \left(p_{ij} + \sum_q p_{iq}\,p_{qj}\right)^2$, where $p_{ij}$ is the share of ego's tie strength invested in contact $j$; the inner sum captures indirect ties routed through mutual contacts $q$, and squaring rewards concentration. The low-constraint positions are the ones network theorists usually care about, since they concentrate the classic structural-hole payoffs: access to non-redundant information, control over what crosses between otherwise separate groups, and the ability to recombine ideas from disconnected clusters. That makes constraint a natural instrument for social-capital studies, innovation research, and any organizational analysis hunting for boundary spanners or entrepreneurial positions. Isolated nodes return `None` because there is no ego network to measure over. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Node "B" brokers between "C" and "D", which aren't connected to each other. A structural hole that gives "B" a low constraint score, while "A" (connected only to "B") has nowhere else to turn and so shows a much higher one: ::: {#541a55a7 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec # Simple network with a broker (B) g = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) # B is the broker .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("B", "D")]) # Note: C and D are not connected ) constraints = g.constraint(return_dict=True) b_id = g.get_id_from_label("B") a_id = g.get_id_from_label("A") constraints[b_id], constraints[a_id] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (0.3333333333333333, 1.0) ``` ::: ::: Node "0"'s two contacts ("1" and "2") are connected to each other, closing off any structural hole, while node "3"'s contacts ("4" and "5") remain disconnected (giving "3" the lower constraint score): ::: {#65a5d8b5 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Compare dense vs. sparse ego networks g = ec.Graph() g.add_nodes(range(6)) # Node 0: connects to 1,2 which are connected (no structural hole) g.add_edges([("0", "1"), ("0", "2"), ("1", "2")]) # Node 3: connects to 4,5 which are NOT connected (structural hole) g.add_edges([("3", "4"), ("3", "5")]) constraints = g.constraint(return_dict=True) node_0_id = g.get_id_from_label("0") node_3_id = g.get_id_from_label("3") constraints[node_0_id], constraints[node_3_id] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (1.125, 0.5) ``` ::: ::: Edge weights change each contact's share of the ego's tie strength. In this weighted triangle "C" puts most of its tie strength into "B", and "B" is itself strongly tied to "A", so "C" is the most constrained; "B", whose strength is spread over two contacts that are only weakly linked to each other, is the least: ::: {#a99bc68b .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = ( ec.Graph(weighted=True) .add_node(label="A") .add_node(label="B") .add_node(label="C") .add_edge("A", "B", weight=5.0) .add_edge("A", "C", weight=1.0) .add_edge("B", "C", weight=3.0) ) scores = g.constraint(return_dict=True) {g.get_label_from_id(nid): round(c, 3) for nid, c in sorted(scores.items())} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` {'A': 1.148, 'B': 0.746, 'C': 1.435} ``` ::: :::
